procedural_history.impugned_order: Judgment and Order dated the 27th October 1953 of the Allahabad High Court in Criminal Reference No. 121 of 1953.
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: The Sessions Judge made a reference to the High Court for quashing the conviction and sentence imposed by the Railway Magistrate, because he believed the case should have been tried by the Panchayati Adalat and that the Railway Magistrate had no jurisdiction. A Single Judge of the High Court did not decide the question of jurisdiction but declined to accept the reference, holding that the revisional jurisdiction of the High Court was discretionary. The Judge then granted a certificate against his own judgment that the case was a fit one for appeal to the Supreme Court.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: The appellant appealed to the Supreme Court by leave granted by the High Court of Allahabad, presumably under Article 134(1)(c) of the Constitution. The Supreme Court dismissed the appeal, holding that the Railway Magistrate had jurisdiction to try the case.

issue.issue_text: Whether a competent bench of the Panchayati Adalat could be properly constituted under the Act to try the present case.

facts: The case involved three accused persons.
One of the three accused was from Jubbalpore in Madhya Pradesh, a location outside the territorial jurisdiction of the U.P. Panchayat Raj Act (the Act).
The case concerned an offense that would normally be triable by a Panchayati Adalat under the Act.
law: Under Section 49 of the Act, a trial bench of the Panchayati Adalat must be formed, which includes a Panch from the Gaon Sabha (village council area) of the accused.
Section 49(4) of the Act authorizes the government to frame rules for constituting special benches for disputes between parties of different "circles or Gaon Sabhas".
Rule 84 was framed under this authority and provided for the constitution of a special bench when one of the parties is a resident of a place not governed by the Act.
Section 55 of the Act bars ordinary courts from trying cases that are cognizable by a Panchayati Adalat, but this bar is only operative if a valid machinery for trial exists under the Act.
application: The court found that a regular bench could not be constituted in strict compliance with Section 49 because one accused was from Madhya Pradesh and did not belong to a "Gaon Sabha" under the U.P. Act.
The court then analyzed the validity of Rule 84, which was intended to solve this problem.

It reasoned that the authority to make rules under Section 49(4) was limited to parties from "circles or Gaon Sabhas" constituted *under the Act*. This authority did not extend to framing a rule for a person belonging to a place outside the state of U.P.
Therefore, the court held that Rule 84, insofar as it applied to a party from outside the state, was *ultra vires* (beyond the powers granted by) Section 49(4).
Since Rule 84 was invalid for this situation, and a regular bench could not be formed, there was no valid legal mechanism under the Act to create a competent bench to try all three accused together.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court rejected the issue, concluding that a competent bench of the Panchayati Adalat could not be properly constituted under the Act to try the case. This was because the specific rule (Rule 84) that would have allowed for the inclusion of an out-of-state accused was invalid, and no other provision could create a valid bench for a case involving an accused from outside the Act's jurisdiction.

issue.issue_text: Whether Rule 84, in so far as it relates to the constitution of a special bench where one of the parties belongs to a place outside the State of U.P., is intra vires.

facts: A criminal case involved three accused persons.
One of the accused was from Madhya Pradesh, a state outside of Uttar Pradesh (U.P.).
The case was to be tried by a Panchayati Adalat, a special court established under the U.P. Panchayat Raj Act.
law: Section 49(2) of the U.P. Panchayat Raj Act sets out the standard procedure for constituting a trial bench, which was impossible to follow in this case as one accused was from outside U.P.

Section 49(4) of the Act grants the government the power to frame rules for constituting special benches for disputes between parties from different "circles or Gaon Sabhas" or "for any other purpose".
Rule 84, created under the authority of Section 49(4), provided for the creation of a special bench when one of the parties was a resident of a place not governed by the Act.
application: The Court first noted that a regular bench could not be formed under Section 49(2) because one accused was from Madhya Pradesh, which has no "Gaon Sabha" under the U.P. Act from which to draw a member for the bench.
The validity of the special bench therefore depended on Rule 84, which in turn depended on the rule-making power granted by Section 49(4).

The Court analyzed the language of Section 49(4) and determined that the phrase "Circles or Gaon Sabhas" referred only to entities constituted under the U.P. Act, meaning it applied to disputes between parties within U.P.

The Court then considered the general catch-all phrase "for any other purpose" and concluded that it could not be construed so broadly as to authorize a rule affecting a person from outside the state.
The Court reasoned that in creating the part of Rule 84 that deals with outsiders, the government had exceeded the specific authority granted to it by the legislature in Section 49(4).
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court held that Rule 84, in so far as it relates to the constitution of a special bench where one of the parties is from outside the State of U.P., is ultra vires (beyond the powers of) the U.P. Panchayat Raj Act. The government did not have the authority under the Act to create such a rule.

issue.issue_text: Whether the jurisdiction of the ordinary courts was excluded by the bar under Section 55 of the Act.

facts: The case involved three accused persons.
One of the accused was from Madhya Pradesh, a place outside the local extent of the U.P. Panchayat Raj Act.
law: Section 55 of the Act bars ordinary courts from taking cognizance of any 'case' which is cognizable by a Panchayati Adalat.
A 'case' under the Act refers to the entire criminal proceeding, involving all accused together.
The jurisdiction of a court of general jurisdiction can be excluded only if the limited jurisdiction of the special court is 'clear and operative'.
Section 49 of the Act requires a bench of the Panchayati Adalat to be constituted with Panches from specific Gaon Sabhas, including the Gaon Sabha of the accused.
The court found Rule 84, which provided for constituting a bench when a party is from outside the state, to be ultra vires (invalid).
application: The bar on jurisdiction under Section 55 applies to the case as a whole, meaning the trial of all three accused together.
For the Panchayati Adalat to have jurisdiction, it must be able to form a valid bench to try the entire case.
Because one accused was from outside the state, a bench could not be properly constituted in compliance with Section 49, as there was no 'Gaon Sabha of the accused' under the Act.
Since Rule 84 was declared invalid, there was no other provision to form a competent bench for this situation.
This lack of a valid mechanism meant that the Panchayati Adalat's jurisdiction was not 'operative' for this specific case.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court decided that the jurisdiction of the ordinary courts was not excluded because no competent bench of the Panchayati Adalat could be constituted to try the case as a whole, due to one of the accused being from outside the state. Since there was no valid machinery for the special court to exercise its jurisdiction, the bar under Section 55 did not apply, and the jurisdiction of the ordinary court remained intact.

arguments.issue_text: Whether a competent bench of the Panchayati Adalat could be properly constituted under the Act to try the present case.
appellant_arguments: The appellant contended that the case should have been tried by the Panchayati Adalat, which implies that a competent bench could be properly constituted to hear the case.
respondent_arguments: A competent bench could not be constituted under the Act because one of the accused resided outside the State of U.P., and there was no provision in the Act to include a Panches from his area in the bench.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the jurisdiction of the ordinary courts was excluded by the bar under Section 55 of the Act.
appellant_arguments: The jurisdiction of the ordinary court (the Railway Magistrate) was excluded by the bar under Section 55 of the Act, as the case was cognizable by a Panchayati Adalat.
respondent_arguments: The bar on jurisdiction under Section 55 is not absolute; it relates to the case as a whole and is only operative if a valid machinery for trial by a Panchayati Adalat exists. Since no competent bench could be formed, the bar does not apply, and the jurisdiction of the ordinary court is not excluded.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: The jurisdiction of a court of general jurisdiction is not excluded by a statute creating a court of limited jurisdiction if the vesting and exercise of that limited jurisdiction is not clear and operative for the specific case. Where there is no validly constituted machinery under the special statute to try a particular case, the jurisdiction of the ordinary court is not barred.
obiter: The court's commentary on the High Court judge's decision to grant a certificate for appeal without first deciding the legal question involved.
The court's speculation that a rule providing for cases where all parties are residents of the same state may be unexceptionable.
The court's express refusal to decide whether a state legislature could, in principle, validly provide for the exercise of jurisdiction over an out-of-state resident by a special court.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: The jurisdiction of the ordinary criminal court was not excluded because a competent bench of the Panchayati Adalat could not be validly constituted to try the case as a whole. Since one of the three accused was from outside the state of U.P., it was impossible to form a bench in compliance with the Act. The bar on the jurisdiction of ordinary courts under Section 55 of the Act is only operative when a valid and adequate machinery for trial by the Panchayati Adalat exists for the entire case, which was not the situation here.
legal_tests_applied: Exclusion of jurisdiction of a court of general jurisdiction, can be brought about by the setting up of a court of limited jurisdiction, in respect of the limited field, only if the vesting and the exercise of that limited jurisdiction is clear and operative.
why_appellant_lost: The appellant's argument that the ordinary court's jurisdiction was barred by Section 55 failed because the bar relates to the 'case as a whole,' involving all accused together, and is only operative if a valid trial machinery exists.
In this case, a valid machinery did not exist because one of the accused was from outside the local extent of the Act, making it impossible to constitute a proper bench under Section 49(2).
The court found that Rule 84, which was intended to address such situations, was ultra vires in so far as it related to constituting a special bench for a party from outside the State of U.P.

Because no competent bench of the Adalat could be formed to try the three accused together, it could have no jurisdiction over the whole case, and therefore the bar under Section 55 could not take away the jurisdiction of the regular criminal court.
why_respondent_won: The bar on jurisdiction under Section 55 is not absolute; it is conditional upon the existence of a valid machinery for trial by a Panchayati Adalat.

A competent bench could not be constituted under the Act because one of the accused belonged to Madhya Pradesh, and there was no valid provision to form a bench to try him along with the other accused.

The jurisdiction of criminal courts under Section 5 of the Code of Criminal Procedure is comprehensive and cannot be held to have been excluded when no valid alternative machinery is set up under the special Act for a particular case.

Since there was no adequate or operative machinery for the exercise of jurisdiction by the Panchayati Adalat in this specific case, the jurisdiction of the court of general jurisdiction (the Railway Magistrate) was not illegally exercised.
policy_considerations: The jurisdiction of a court of general jurisdiction cannot be excluded unless the alternative court of limited jurisdiction is clearly and operatively established to handle the specific case. This prevents a jurisdictional vacuum where an offence might go untried due to procedural gaps in a special law.
